title: From the Human Genome Project to Clinical Genomics
summary: The technological revolution that made whole-genome sequencing a clinical tool in 25 years.

content_blocks.text: The Human Genome Project (HGP), completed in 2003 after 13 years and $3 billion, sequenced the first reference human genome. Today, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) costs under $500 and can be completed in 24–48 hours. This 6-million-fold cost reduction over two decades is faster than Moore's Law and has fundamentally transformed medicine.

content_blocks.text: First-generation Sanger sequencing (1977) reads short fragments accurately but slowly. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) platforms (Illumina, Ion Torrent) perform massively parallel short-read sequencing — cheap and high-throughput but struggle with repetitive regions. Third-generation long-read platforms (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore) sequence single molecules in real time, resolving structural variants and repeat expansions that short reads miss.

Clinical applications span the continuum from targeted single-gene tests (e.g., CFTR for cystic fibrosis) to multigene panels (e.g., 80-gene hereditary cancer panel), whole-exome sequencing (WES, ~2% of genome), and whole-genome sequencing (WGS, 100%). The clinical utility — not just the technology capability — drives which test is appropriate.
